name: phase2_tier3_covert
_comment: Tier 3: the receiver reads nothing at all. It runs its own fixed
instruction stream and times it with rdtsc, so unlike tier 2 there is no
file to revoke and no interface a container can decline to mount. That
makes it the hardest of the three to defend against.
Same preconditions as tier 2, for the same reason: Config-B, and ten
victim threads so that something is actually limiting. A hand check found
the receiver's own workload stretched from 1,401,990 TSC under the all-zero
operand to 1,639,579 under all-ones, a 17% dilation, against an idle
baseline of 1,353,437.
This is the second pass. The first (results/20260903-185812) decoded 1 bit/s
at BER 0.000 in all three repeats but had its A/A gate fail, and the reason
was a defect in the payload rather than in the channel: --random-bits drew
i.i.d. bits, one repeat drew 7 ones in 8, and a decoder whose output is
skewed the same way then scores well on a transmission carrying nothing.
Payloads are balanced by construction now, which makes the expected BER
exactly 0.5 for any biased-but-independent decode, so an A/A can only beat
chance by actually recovering information.
Payloads are also larger. The old A/A carried 8 distinct bits repeated over
4 frames -- 32 comparisons against 8 independent truths, far too few for a
per-run gate to resolve chance. aa_0256ms exists to buy statistical power
cheaply (bits are 4x cheaper per second there), aa_1000ms to control the
rate the headline result is quoted at.
500 us per sample is a compromise: shorter samples resolve a chip better
but each carries proportionally more rdtsc and lfence overhead, and the
fences are not optional (see the note in rx_timing.c).
